lead_note: Epoch AI's Capabilities Index put Chinese models an average of seven months behind U.S. models from 2023 through 2025, with a range of four to fourteen months depending on the milestone. Newer point estimates cluster lower and tighter: NIST's evaluation of DeepSeek V4 Pro put it about eight months behind, AISI's cyber work put leading open-weight models four to seven months back, and Mozilla's September 2026 tracker, as reported by Android Headlines, says 4.4 months. Seven is a round default at the high end of recent estimates. It only sets the starting balance: no price on the menu depends on it. You can change it on the assumptions page.

policies.name: Critical safety incident reporting
policies.practice: When something goes badly wrong, such as stolen model weights or a model helping to cause serious harm, the lab reports it to the state within 15 days. If lives are at immediate risk, it has 24 hours.
policies.why: A report is filed after an incident, so it never holds up a model. The only cost is the staff time to set up the process and write reports, about two days.

policies.how: Placeholder: about two days of compliance staff time. There is no data on this.
policies.short: Tell the state within 15 days when something goes seriously wrong. 24 hours if it is imminent.
policies.trigger: Frontier developers (models above 10^26 FLOP).
policies.uncertainty: None worth naming. The only cost is a lawyer's afternoon.
requires: Report a critical safety incident to the state within 15 days of discovering it (California SB 53).
Report within 24 hours if the incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury.
EU Code of Practice signatories report serious incidents on a 2, 5, 10 or 15 day clock depending on severity.
SB 1047 would have required 72 hours.
policies.baseline: OpenAI and Anthropic already have incident processes under their own frameworks, and both are now legally bound by SB 53 in California. Nothing in the requirement touches training, internal use or release.
policies.reasoning:
A reporting deadline starts after an incident happens. It does not stop any model from being trained, used or shipped. The work is writing a report, which happens asynchronously and in parallel with everything else.
There is no plausible mechanism by which a 15-day or even a 72-hour reporting window delays a frontier training run or a launch. The rubric charges asynchronous paperwork at zero, and this is the cleanest case of it on the menu.
Staff time is not free. The engineers and policy staff who do this are the same people who would otherwise be building the next model, so we charge about two days of the U.S. frontier for it.
policies.steelman: A reporting regime creates a record that regulators and plaintiffs can use later, which could make labs more cautious about internal deployments of capable models. That caution, not the filing, is where a cost would come from. We see no evidence of it so far and it would be a cost of liability exposure rather than of the reporting rule itself.

OpenAI's Preparedness Framework is on version 2, with a companion Frontier Governance Framework written to map onto SB 53 and the EU Code. Google DeepMind and xAI publish frontier safety frameworks. The requirement codifies what every covered lab already publishes.
policies.reasoning:
The framework already exists at every lab this applies to. The incremental work is legal review and a compliance function, neither of which sits on the path from a training run to a model.
The only mechanism for a lead cost is behavioral: a lab that is legally bound to its own framework might hold a launch to satisfy a threshold it set for itself. That is a cost of the framework's content, not of publishing it, and labs write their own content. We charge a few days at the high end to cover launches held for a compliance sign-off.
Staff time is not free. The engineers and policy staff who do this are the same people who would otherwise be building the next model, so we charge about three days of the U.S. frontier for it.
policies.steelman: Anthropic's RSP v3.0 explicitly moved away from hard pre-deployment gates toward public goals it grades itself against. A law that makes a framework binding removes that flexibility. If a lab's own threshold is crossed at an awkward moment, a binding framework could force a delay the voluntary version would not. The cost is real but it is the cost of a threshold, and it is priced under the evaluation and safety-case items.

Two small residual risks. First, a required document can slip a launch by days if evaluation results arrive late. Second, the requirement is "before or concurrently with" deployment, and deployment under SB 53 means making the model available to any third party, which includes trusted-access programs. Staff time is not free. The engineers and policy staff who do this are the same people who would otherwise be building the next model, so we charge about three days of the U.S. frontier for it.

policies.steelman: The definition of deployment is broad. GovAI found that in the first five months of 2026, the frontier models withheld from general release were instead given to select entities under trusted-access programs. If a transparency report is required before any third party touches the model, those programs would have to wait for the write-up. That could cost a week or two on the access clock per model, and it is why the high end of the range is a week.

policies.reasoning:
Internal evaluations already run on every frontier release. AISI's published estimate is that automated evaluations complete in a few days, with a one-to-two-week end-to-end process including reporting, and AISI designs its evaluations in advance so they can run immediately. Labs can run most of the suite on earlier checkpoints and rerun a subset on the final one.
A mandate changes two things. It removes the option to skip evaluations on a fast release, and it can push a launch a few days while results are written up. Neither touches training or internal use. The central price to China's access is three days per generation; the high end is two weeks for a lab whose final checkpoint differs enough from its proxies to need a full rerun.
Staff time is not free. The engineers and policy staff who do this are the same people who would otherwise be building the next model, so we charge about five days of the U.S. frontier for it.

That gate is priced separately, but a critic would say the two cannot be separated in practice.

The model exists before the evaluator sees it. Training is done, internal deployment can continue, and the lab can begin the successor. So the U.S. internal frontier does not move.

Making the report a precondition adds the report-writing tail plus whatever access time the evaluator insists on. We price one week of added release delay per generation, with a range from nothing (the lab shares a checkpoint earlier) to three weeks (the lab shares late and waits).
At the high end for the U.S. frontier, we charge a week for a lab that, under the requirement, delays internal deployment until evaluation is complete. Nothing in the requirement demands that, but some labs may choose it.
Staff time is not free. The engineers and policy staff who do this are the same people who would otherwise be building the next model, so we charge about four days of the U.S. frontier for it.

combos.name: California SB 1047 (as vetoed)
combos.practice: California's 2024 bill that Governor Newsom vetoed. It required a safety plan before training, a kill switch, yearly audits, 72-hour incident reports and ID checks on cloud customers, and banned releasing a model with an unreasonable risk of catastrophe.
combos.why: Most parts matched what labs already did. The ban on risky releases and the audits add some delay and staff time, about nine days in total.

for.what: wrote the bill, which passed the legislature in 2024.

against.what: vetoed it, saying it applied stringent standards to even basic functions, 2024.

against.who: Chamber of Progress, NetChoice, R Street and others
against.what: signed a joint letter urging a veto, 2024.
argued against it, as reported by TechCrunch, 2024.

combos.how: Its parts cost about 12 days of staff time, including a small delay from the ban on risky releases. ID checks on cloud customers give back about 3 days. Net: about 9 days.
combos.short: The bill everyone fought about. Pre-training protocol, kill switch, annual audits, 72-hour incidents, compute KYC.
combos.trigger: Models above 10^26 FLOP costing more than $100M to train.
combos.uncertainty: How a lab would have interpreted the duty not to release a model posing an unreasonable risk of critical harm, and whether a self-certified pre-training protocol ever delays a run.
requires: Before training: cybersecurity protections, full shutdown capability, and a written safety and security protocol, published in redacted form and sent to the Attorney General (self-certified, no approval).
Before release: assess whether the model could cause or enable critical harm, retain test records, and do not release if there is an unreasonable risk of critical harm.
From 2026: annual independent third-party audit, published in redacted form.
Report safety incidents to the Attorney General within 72 hours.
Compute providers: know-your-customer and shutdown capability for frontier-scale customers.
Whistleblower protections and an anonymous internal channel.
Penalties up to 10% of training compute cost for a first harmful violation, 30% thereafter.
combos.baseline: Every obligation except the audits, the KYC rules and the release prohibition was already voluntary practice at the covered labs by 2024. SB 53, enacted a year later, kept the framework, transparency and incident provisions and dropped the shutdown mandate, pre-training protocol, audits and compute-based penalties.
combos.reasoning:
Price the components. Framework, shutdown, incident reporting, audits, KYC and whistleblower protections are all starters: near zero on both clocks.
Two provisions have teeth. The pre-training protocol is self-certified, so it does not gate a run the way a licensing regime would; it is a document the lab writes before starting. We charge days at most. The release prohibition is the real one: a lab may not release a model that poses an unreasonable risk of critical harm. That is a standard, not a procedure. In practice it makes the lab's own evaluation-and-mitigation loop legally binding, which we price like the triggered red-team item at a reduced rate: a week of release delay centrally, three weeks at the high end for a model that trips the standard.
Net: three days of U.S. lead centrally, half a month at the very worst, and a small China-side benefit from KYC on compute. The bill's price on this menu is about a fortieth of the rhetoric around it.
The bundle also carries the staff time of its parts. Those overlap, since the same compliance team handles all of them, so we charge a bit less than their sum.

rubric.charge: the release prohibition, priced as a partial trigger

combos.steelman: The compute-based penalty, up to 30% of training cost, creates liability that scales with ambition. A rational lab facing that exposure would evaluate more, mitigate more and release later, and the marginal caution is not captured by pricing the procedures. The undefined "unreasonable risk" standard is where the cost hides, and a court could read it in ways the lab cannot plan around. Newsom's veto message did not say the bill was expensive; it said it targeted the wrong models. The lead cost was never the strongest argument against it.

combos.practice: Europe's rules for the most powerful models, enforceable since August 2026. Labs must test for serious risks, give outside testers time with the model, report incidents, and file a report before release.

combos.baseline: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Amazon and Microsoft signed the full Code; xAI signed the safety chapter; Meta did not sign. GovAI found no model release delayed or withheld from the EU in the first five months of 2026, before fines applied. The obligations are now enforceable and it is too early to see their effect.
combos.reasoning:
The EU bundle is the heaviest of the real bills because it is the only one that puts independent external evaluation and a suggested evaluation period on the path to market. Everything else in it is a starter.
The binding constraint is the Model Report, which must exist before market and must reflect evaluations that the Code says should get at least 20 business days where appropriate. That is the evaluator-window item, priced as the increment over current practice: two weeks of release delay centrally, ranging from one week to five. Because the U.S. frontier is not the EU market, a lab could in principle release in the U.S. first and the EU later, which GovAI's data shows was the pattern under GDPR. Then the price on the access clock shrinks toward zero and the cost becomes purely commercial. We price for a lab that keeps global launches synchronized.
The U.S. internal frontier is not touched by any of it. The high end of a week covers a lab that holds internal rollout for the Model Report.
The bundle also carries the staff time of its parts. Those overlap, since the same compliance team handles all of them, so we charge a bit less than their sum.

If labs do not want to ship the U.S. first and the EU five weeks later, the whole delay lands on the global release.

combos.reasoning:
This is the independent-evaluation item with the government as evaluator and no time limit. The model exists; training and internal use are untouched; release waits.
The uncertainty is throughput. A DOE program with classified testing that has to clear four labs' releases could take a week or two per model if it runs like CAISI, or two months if it runs like a federal certification. On the U.S. clock, three days centrally and two weeks at the high end for a lab that holds internal deployment pending the government's result.

The bundle also carries the staff time of its parts. Those overlap, since the same compliance team handles all of them, so we charge a bit less than their sum.
combos.steelman: A mandatory federal program with a $1M-a-day penalty is a licensing regime for deployment. The first time it backs up, every lab waits. The first time it finds something, remediation is negotiated with a federal agency rather than decided internally. The bill's two-month high end could be its normal operating state.
